description: We're The Hotspot, a team of five university students from the University of Stirling, Ras Al Khaimah campus (UAE), taking on "Be an Earth System Trend Detective"
summary:
TerraTrace is an interactive Earth-system investigation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps anyone explore how the planet is changing, and test whether an apparent trend is real before drawing conclusions.

Using NASA Earth science datasets (POWER/MERRA-2, GPCP, GISTEMP and GLDAS), TerraTrace analyses temperature, rainfall and soil moisture from 2001 to 2024. Every trend is tested with the Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence interval, a correction for autocorrelation, false-discovery-rate control and a step-change check, to separate meaningful change from statistical noise.

What makes TerraTrace different is cross-dataset validation. Each trend is re-tested against a second NASA record, and the app reports agreement, disagreement and uncertainty rather than presenting every result as certain. For example, one NASA record shows the Central African Republic cooling significantly, while NASA’s station-based record shows warming. TerraTrace flags the conflict, traces the “cooling” to a sudden 2007 data jump, and keeps it out of its rankings.

Users explore any place on an interactive 3D globe, examine tested trends and unusual years, and export fact sheets and investigation reports with data and citations. It’s free, needs no login and works on a phone.

TerraTrace makes Earth-system science accessible while teaching people to question, test and understand environmental evidence.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraTrace is a free, browser-based investigation platform that lets anyone pick any place on Earth and find out whether its climate is really changing. Users click a location on an interactive 3D globe, search a city, or choose a one-click example, then pick an indicator: air temperature, rainfall or root-zone soil moisture, 2001-2024. TerraTrace returns a tested trend for that place, says how confident we can be, checks it against a second NASA record, and lets the user export the evidence as a fact sheet, a nine-step investigation report, CSV data and ready-made APA, Harvard and BibTeX citations.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline collects and cleans NASA data on a 5-degree global grid. It made 6,162 requests to NASA POWER (MERRA-2) and processed 576 monthly files from NASA GES DISC (GPCP V3.3 rainfall and GLDAS-2.1 soil moisture), plus NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 temperature. It removes invalid fill values, never fills gaps by guessing, and converts monthly data to annual values to remove the seasonal cycle. Every place is then tested with the methods climate scientists use:

- Mann-Kendall trend test, with the Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation

- Sen's slope with a 95% confidence interval

- Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across the whole map

- A step-change test that catches "trends" that are really one sudden jump

- Detection of unusual years

The same statistics run in Python and in the browser, and the two agree on all 5,846 trend tests.

CROSS-DATASET VALIDATION

What makes TerraTrace different is that no trend is trusted on one record alone. Each trend is re-tested on a second NASA record: temperature against GISTEMP (stations), rainfall against MERRA-2, and soil moisture against GLDAS. The app then gives one of six verdicts, from "Independent Verification" to "Cross-Dataset Divergence". For example, MERRA-2 shows the Central African Republic cooling significantly, while NASA's station-based GISTEMP shows warming. TerraTrace flags the conflict, traces the "cooling" to a sudden drop around 2007, and keeps it out of its rankings. Where records share inputs, we say so, and we report weak results honestly: only 17 of 336 significant rainfall trends survive map-wide false-discovery control.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

NASA's Earth data is free, but turning it into a defensible claim normally takes coding, GIS software and statistics. TerraTrace removes that barrier. Students can turn a question into a cited, defensible answer. Teachers can set investigations on any place on Earth. Anyone with a phone can explore it, with no login. Above all, we want people to learn to question evidence before believing it. Most tools show you the data. TerraTrace teaches you to question it.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globe, Chart.js for charts, GSAP for animation, and d3-geo with topojson and Natural Earth borders for country averages.

- Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, pandas, requests and netCDF4.

- Data: NASA POWER, NASA GES DISC (GPCP, GLDAS) and NASA GISS (GISTEMP), accessed with NASA Earthdata login.

- Hosting and code: Cloudflare Pages, and GitHub under the MIT licence.

- Hardware: standard laptops only; the app runs fully in the browser and works offline when run locally.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

TerraTrace treats climate data like a detective case: discover a trend, test it, call a second witness, investigate disagreements, and produce a citable finding. Other tools show a single dataset as fact. TerraTrace shows uncertainty openly, flags data artefacts, and turns every result into a step-by-step investigation that a non-specialist can follow.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific integrity: we report confidence intervals, autocorrelation, multiple testing and how independent the datasets are, and never fill gaps or overstate results.

- Accessibility: plain-language explanations, a glossary of terms, a mobile-friendly design and no login.

- Transparency: every number links to its NASA source, with open code and documented methods.

- Limitations: a 5-degree grid and a 24-year record are stated clearly in the app and the documentation.
